extracted.intended_audience: city reporters, city editors, and journalism students learning interview and beat-reporting techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting, conducting, and writing interviews (including symposiums/public-opinion samplings) and on developing/covering club and lodge beats for a city newspaper. Covers topic selection, sampling, question design, structure/formatting, and beat cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic selection — local relevance and news peg
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose interview subjects based on actions, trends, forecasts, or persons elsewhere that could be duplicated in or affect the community; or on a particular person of present/past prominence; or on society-page notices and one-paragraph news items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: another city's abandoning parking meters leads to 'Should our city give up or retain its meters?'; an ordinance elsewhere prompts 'Will this action cause criminals to come to our city?'; forecasts (e.g., textile employment upturn) become 'Will our textile mills share in the better business?' Use any action, trend, prediction, or notable person as the news peg. Convert distant events into local 'folo' (follow-up) interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person interviews — match subject to topic expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict interviewees to subjects about which they naturally may be well informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asking a well-spoken person about topics they have no basis to discuss (example: do not ask a minister who never traveled to the Arctic about freak weather in Iceland). Prefer sources whose background gives them authority or unique perspective on the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overusing the same sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not interview the same two or three helpful persons repeatedly; diversify interview sources so coverage isn't repetitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a broad roster of knowledgeable residents so the paper doesn't run repeated 'Conrad Asserts' or 'Conrad Declares' headlines; locate new sources when current ones are overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symposium/sample selection — choose persons with interesting stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Select persons whose positions or circumstances make their opinions interesting and meaningful to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including visitors or persons without a stake (example: a visiting judge's opinion is uninteresting if he has no local knowledge). Choose interviewees representing different viewpoints and circumstances so each quotation contributes distinct reasoning rather than repeating the same sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding uniform, redundant comments in group interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent a symposium from being clogged with comments that all read alike or convey identical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan sampling and questions so quotations vary in reason and phrasing; pick diversified situations among respondents to avoid a chorus of 'Me, too.' Inadequate planning leads to half-columns of identical-meaning quotations — an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symposium lead duties (four essential functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A symposium lead must: (1) summarize the results of the interviews (specific, not general); (2) recount the news that provoked the symposium; (3) summarize the majority view and its bases; (4) summarize the minority view and its bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific in (1) (e.g., 'Five out of seven persons interviewed opposed...'). For (2) recall and restate the provoking news so hurried readers understand context. For (3) and (4) give the bases for each viewpoint; generally avoid names and direct quotes in the lead. These duties provide a framework for the details that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and logistics — find diverse respondents and plan itinerary
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which respondents will have active interest and differing viewpoints; know where to find them and plan an itinerary to minimize legwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List 'breeds' of affected people (taxi driver, shopper, truck driver, merchant, parking-lot operator, policeman, pedestrian, etc.) and determine where they congregate (lunchrooms, stores, clinics). This foresight yields varied responses and efficient fieldwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question design — universal question plus tailored questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a universal question to keep all interviews on topic and a particularized question for each person to draw out the viewpoint characteristic of that group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal example: 'What do you think of Judge Hammill's proposal?' Tailored examples: out-of-town shopper: 'Will you continue to come here or go to Junctionville?'; in-town shopper: 'Will you drive as heretofore or take the bus?' Individualized questions prevent a chorus of identical replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent grammatical/structural treatment across interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose one method of presenting individual interviews and use it uniformly so readers can easily follow where one interview ends and the next begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three acceptable structures are given (see separate rubric entries); mixing methods hashes the symposium and confuses readers. Parallel syntax for all interviews is the keynote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview format option A — name + identification + sentence/brief quote
rubrics_metrics.description: Present each interview as: Name, identification, and a sentence or brief quoted paragraph (e.g., 'Henry Wade, truck driver — It'll be like going back to the old days...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method gives a clear break between interviews and is almost impossible to misread. Whether to enclose quotations in quote marks depends on the paper's style sheet. Recommended when maximum emphasis on breaks is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview format option B — lead quotation split by identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a strong quotation, then attribute it with the interviewee's name and identification (quotation split by the name/ID).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage: brings a strong quotation to the front of the paragraph. Danger: blocks interviews less completely and risks typesetting/quote-mark errors (e.g., linotype operators careless about opening/closing quotes). Use when the quote is the most compelling element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview format option C — summary followed by name/ID and direct quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a paraphrase/summary sentence, then give the name/ID and follow with a direct quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often best when long quotations must be presented. The paraphrase provides a clear break between interviews and helps smooth presentation of longer quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead by example — sample lead for a symposium
rubrics_metrics.description: Model lead demonstrates the four duties with numbered components: (1) specific summary of results, (2) recounting the provoking announcement, (3) majority view and reasons, (4) minority view and reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this template (as shown in the text) for training/analysis; e.g., 'Two days in jail is too harsh... This was the view of five out of seven persons questioned yesterday about (2) the announcement by Judge E. A. Hammill...' The example shows how to compress background and viewpoints efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel syntax and uniform presentation — avoid mixed styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain the same grammatical structure across all interviews in a symposium; mixing methods confuses readers and undermines clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixed approach produces a 'cowpath' structure that disorients readers and was a principal reason symposia went out of fashion. Consistency lets readers know what to expect next and conserves attention for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter empathy — put yourself in interviewee's place
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter gets the best, most meaningful quotations by imagining the world from the interviewee's perspective and handling that person accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop familiarity with a wide range of residents so the reporter can present informed viewpoints across diverse topics (examples of different people and subjects are given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivating a club/lodge beat — invent and develop a beat
rubrics_metrics.description: If no regular beat exists, the reporter may 'invent' a beat (e.g., clubs and lodges) by cultivating stories and contacts until the editor supports a regular part-time beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may require work on the reporter's own time. Regular, steady volume of club/lodge news justifies making it a beat and can build the reporter's specialist status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clubs/lodges are newsworthy — readership interest and names
rubrics_metrics.description: Club and lodge news is worthwhile because memberships include thousands of readers who enjoy seeing names and local activities in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People are clannish and loyal; even casual readers like to see acquaintances mentioned. Emphasize names and human-interest hooks to reach both members and casual readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use names and a feature lead to attract casual readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for names for inclusion, and lead with a feature angle that translates lodge events into language that appeals to casual readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't open with bland generalizations ('A busy winter season has been planned...'); instead specify what makes the season busy. Example: instead of 'The Elks have paid the last $900...' use 'The mortgage won't worry the Elks any more' to hook readers worried about mortgages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generalizations and puffery; be specific and not promotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vague, hard-to-visualize phrasing or wording that appears to be free advertising for the lodge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'A busy winter season has been planned' is a poor lead; change generalizations into specific statements describing exactly what is planned. Avoid phrasing that suggests boosterism or favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and use correct lodge/club nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: Master the specific titles and terminology of clubs and lodges to avoid embarrassing errors that undermine credibility with members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: calling the 'right supporter' the 'right assistant' or the Masonic 'worshipful master' the 'grand' will signal ignorance and kill the story's credibility. Accurate nomenclature is essential for acceptance by members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid favoritism — equitable coverage across groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not judge story value solely by club size; avoid any semblance of partiality in length or prominence of coverage among similar organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one group's election gets half a column and another similar group's election gets two inches, complaints will follow. Be scrupulous against favoritism, especially among groups with religious or semireligious backgrounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never mock or use sarcasm about clubs/lodges
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make fun of clubs or lampoon their ceremonies; sarcasm alienates members and provokes lasting anger at the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even mild sarcasm can make every member angry for months. Respect ceremonial language and avoid condescending reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staking out the field — research beyond directories
rubrics_metrics.description: Discover the full list of organizations in the city by persistent digging; directories are often incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reporter should iteratively build knowledge of standard groups and then uncover specialized or small groups whose memberships overlap. Relying solely on the directory risks missing many clubs (examples: Saharan Camels, Philatelic and Numismatic Club).
